CHARACTER.name: The Conscious Subject

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Bad-Faith Actor

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Free Agent

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Observer

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Observed Self

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Choosing Self

CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Situated Individual
CHARACTER.description: An explicitly analytical sample figure representing freedom exercised within circumstances that the individual did not freely create.
CHARACTER.source: Analytical sample context for Being and Nothingness

CHARACTER.name: The Reflective Self

CONCEPTS.definition: Sartre's philosophical category for being considered independently of the self-transcending structure associated with consciousness.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: Sartre's category associated with consciousness as a form of being that relates to itself and can project possibilities beyond its present state.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: A central ontological concept connected with negation, absence, consciousness, and the possibility of distancing oneself from what simply is.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: A form of self-deception in which a person attempts to evade the tension between freedom and the factual conditions of existence.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: The capacity of consciousness to project possibilities and make choices within the circumstances of a concrete situation.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: The concrete facts and conditions of one's existence that are encountered as already given.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: The capacity of consciousness to reach beyond its immediately given condition toward possibilities, projects, and meanings.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: The dimension of existence disclosed through relationships with other consciousnesses and awareness of oneself as perceived by others.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: Sartre's analysis of encountering another consciousness through an experience in which one becomes aware of oneself as an object for another.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

CONCEPTS.definition: The existential burden associated with choices and projects undertaken by a free individual within a situation.
CONCEPTS.source: Study context for Being and Nothingness

GLOSARY.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with being and what it means for something to exist.
GLOSARY.etymology: From Greek roots relating to being and study.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Ontology provides the framework for asking what distinguishes consciousness from other forms of being.

GLOSARY.definition: A philosophical approach concerned with describing structures of experience as they appear to consciousness.
GLOSARY.etymology: From Greek-derived terms referring to appearance and study.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Phenomenology directs attention toward the structures through which experience becomes meaningful.

GLOSARY.definition: The given conditions of existence that form part of a person's concrete situation.
GLOSARY.etymology: Derived from fact and philosophical terminology concerning factual existence.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Facticity describes circumstances that must be encountered even when they do not completely determine future choices.

GLOSARY.definition: The movement beyond a present condition toward possibilities, meanings, goals, or projects.
GLOSARY.etymology: From Latin transcendere, meaning to climb beyond or surpass.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Transcendence describes how consciousness reaches toward possibilities beyond its present condition.

GLOSARY.definition: The act or structure of denying, excluding, or recognizing that something is not the case.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Negation becomes philosophically significant when consciousness recognizes an absence rather than merely another object.

GLOSARY.definition: Awareness through which the world, oneself, and possible actions are experienced.
GLOSARY.etymology: From Latin conscientia, associated with shared or internal knowledge.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Consciousness is examined as an active relation to the world rather than a passive container of experiences.

GLOSARY.definition: The capacity to choose and project possibilities within a concrete situation.
GLOSARY.etymology: From Old English freodom, associated with the condition of being free.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Freedom does not require an absence of circumstances but concerns how possibilities are pursued within them.

GLOSARY.definition: Accountability associated with one's choices, projects, actions, and their consequences.
GLOSARY.etymology: Derived from Latin respondere, meaning to answer or respond.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Responsibility becomes difficult to escape when refusing to choose is itself embedded in a situation requiring action.

GLOSARY.definition: Experience from the perspective of a conscious subject.
GLOSARY.etymology: Derived from subject and ultimately from Latin subjectus.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Subjectivity cannot be understood only by describing the individual as an external object.

GLOSARY.definition: A philosophical tradition concerned with human existence, freedom, choice, responsibility, meaning, and concrete lived experience.
GLOSARY.etymology: Derived from existence, ultimately from Latin exsistere, meaning to emerge or come into being.
GLOSARY.contextSentence: Existentialism places questions of freedom and responsibility within the circumstances of lived human existence.

PASSAGES.title: The Empty Chair
PASSAGES.passageText: He entered expecting to find his friend and noticed the empty chair immediately. The absence was not another object in the room, yet it reorganized everything he saw.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: A Fixed Identity
PASSAGES.passageText: He described himself entirely through his occupation, as though the title had existed before his choices and would continue deciding them afterward. The certainty was comforting because it made alternatives disappear.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: The Unchosen Situation
PASSAGES.passageText: Many facts had been decided without him: the place, the history, the limitations, the circumstances. Yet none of these facts could complete the unfinished question of what he would do with them.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: Being Seen
PASSAGES.passageText: Alone, the gesture had seemed insignificant. Once another person noticed it, the same movement returned to him as something visible, judged, and no longer entirely his own.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: Possibility
PASSAGES.passageText: The present situation described what existed but could not fully prescribe what came next. Possibility appeared in the distance between circumstances and choice.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: The Excuse
PASSAGES.passageText: He wanted the situation to contain an instruction that would remove responsibility from him. Instead every explanation eventually returned to the uncomfortable fact that an action still had to be chosen.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: Object and Subject
PASSAGES.passageText: He could describe the body as though observing an object, yet lived experience refused to remain outside the description. The body was both encountered and inhabited.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: Another Freedom
PASSAGES.passageText: The other person would not remain inside the role assigned to them. Their freedom interrupted every attempt to transform the relationship into something completely predictable.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: The Project
PASSAGES.passageText: A choice acquired meaning through the future toward which it pointed. Action therefore revealed not merely what had happened, but something about the world the person was attempting to create.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

PASSAGES.title: Unfinished Self
PASSAGES.passageText: No description seemed able to close the account permanently. The past constrained the next decision without becoming identical to it, leaving the self continually unfinished.
PASSAGES.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

QUOTES.quote: Freedom becomes difficult precisely when circumstances cannot make the choice for us.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on freedom within concrete situations.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: A role can describe what we do without exhausting what we are able to become.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on identity, social roles, and bad faith.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: Absence becomes meaningful when consciousness expected a presence.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on negation, expectation, and nothingness.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: To be seen is to discover that another perspective on us exists beyond our control.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on the philosophical significance of the look and being-for-others.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: The facts of a life establish conditions without writing the final sentence.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on the relationship between facticity and freedom.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: Self-deception becomes attractive when freedom feels heavier than certainty.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on bad faith as an attempted escape from existential freedom.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: Another person's freedom resists becoming a permanent object inside our plans.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on relationships between independent consciousnesses.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: Responsibility begins where explanations stop pretending to be decisions.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on agency, choice, and responsibility.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: The self remains unfinished because possibility accompanies every present definition.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on identity, possibility, and transcendence.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

QUOTES.quote: Existence becomes a philosophical problem when living requires choosing what existing will mean.
QUOTES.analysis: An original reflection on existentialism, freedom, and the creation of meaning through action.
QUOTES.author: Sumaq Yachay Sample

RELATIONS.description: This reading association links The Conscious Subject (An explicitly analytical sample figure representing the conscious individual examined through Sartre's distinctions between being, nothingness, freedom, and self-awareness.) with The Other (An explicitly analytical sample figure representing another consciousness whose presence introduces recognition, objectification, conflict, and interpersonal awareness.). The theme “Being” and subtheme “Existence and the structure of reality” guide the comparison; the passage “The Empty Chair” supplies context from the book itself. It is an interpretive connection based on these entries, not a claim that the characters share a scene.

ASSOCIATIONS.description: The definition of “Being-in-itself” (“Sartre's philosophical category for being considered independently of the self-transcending structure associated with consciousness.”) can be read in relation to “Being-for-itself” (“Sartre's category associated with consciousness as a form of being that relates to itself and can project possibilities beyond its present state.”). The theme Being and subtheme Existence and the structure of reality, together with the passage “The Empty Chair”, place this conceptual connection in the book’s reading context.
ASSOCIATIONS.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

ASSOCIATIONS.description: The definition of “Nothingness” (“A central ontological concept connected with negation, absence, consciousness, and the possibility of distancing oneself from what simply is.”) can be read in relation to “Bad faith” (“A form of self-deception in which a person attempts to evade the tension between freedom and the factual conditions of existence.”). The theme Nothingness and subtheme Negation and the activity of consciousness, together with the passage “A Fixed Identity”, place this conceptual connection in the book’s reading context.
